summary: Defines a method for a protected resource to ask an OAuth 2.0 authorization server whether a token is currently active and to get information about it. This conveys the authorization context from the server to the resource.

plainLanguage.summary: Token introspection is a question one web service asks another about an access token: is this token still valid, what does it allow, and who was it issued to. The answer comes back as a small JSON object, so the service holding the token does not need to understand its format.

questions: how to check if an oauth token is active
what does the active field mean in token introspection
how to secure the introspection endpoint
subtitle: Lets a protected resource ask the authorization server what a token means.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 tokens are opaque to clients, and OAuth 2.0 has no way for a protected resource to ask the authorization server whether a token is still valid, what it is allowed to do, and who authorized it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an introspection endpoint that a protected resource calls over HTTP POST with the token, and that returns a JSON object whose active field says whether the token is live, along with optional metadata such as the scope, the client, the subject and the expiry.
tldr.outcome: A resource server can base an authorization decision on the authorization context of the token without understanding the token format itself, whether the token is a random string or a signed structured token.

today: RFC 7662 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. Its appendix notes that use with proof-of-possession tokens is left to a future extension.

sections.title: Why a Resource Server Asks
sections.content:
In OAuth 2.0 the contents of tokens are opaque to clients, so a client does not need to know anything about the content or structure of the token. A large amount of metadata may still be attached to a token, such as its current validity, its approved scopes, and information about the context in which it was issued. That metadata is often vital to a protected resource making an authorization decision based on the token it has been given.

OAuth 2.0 does not define a protocol for the resource server to learn this information, so several approaches grew up to fill the gap. One is to use a structured token format such as a JSON Web Token (JWT), so that the information travels inside the token itself. Another is a proprietary mechanism between services, such as a shared database or a protected enterprise service bus, that carries the token information out of band.

This specification defines a protocol that lets an authorized protected resource query the authorization server for the metadata of a given token. The metadata says whether the token is currently active, meaning it has expired or been revoked, what rights of access the token carries, usually through OAuth 2.0 scopes, and the authorization context in which it was granted, including who authorized it and which client it was issued to.

Introspection works whether or not the information is carried in the token itself, so it can be used alongside structured token values or independently of them. A protected resource can also introspect the token in a particular authorization decision context, and take the metadata into account for that decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of carrying the facts about a token have grown up: pack them inside the token, or share them through a private channel between the services. Introspection is a third, standard way: ask the server that issued the token.

sections.title: The Introspection Request
sections.content:
The introspection endpoint is an OAuth 2.0 endpoint that takes a parameter representing a token and returns a JSON document describing the metadata around it, including whether the token is currently active. What counts as active depends on the authorization server, but it is commonly a token that this server issued, has not expired, has not been revoked, and is valid for use at the protected resource making the call. The endpoint MUST be protected by a transport-layer security mechanism, and how a protected resource discovers where the endpoint lives is outside the scope of this specification.

The protected resource calls the endpoint with an HTTP POST, sending parameters as application/x-www-form-urlencoded data. The token parameter is required. For an access token it is the access_token value returned by the token endpoint of OAuth 2.0; for a refresh token it is the refresh_token value. Other token types are out of scope.

The token_type_hint parameter is optional. It is a hint about the type of the token, which the server may use to speed up the lookup. If the server cannot find the token using the hint, it MUST widen the search across all the token types it supports, and it MAY ignore the hint entirely, for example when it can detect the type by itself. The values for this field come from the OAuth Token Type Hints registry defined in OAuth Token Revocation.

The endpoint MAY accept other optional parameters to give the server more context, for instance the IP address of the client reaching the protected resource, so that the server can judge whether the right client is likely to be presenting the token. The definition of such parameters is left to service documentation or to extensions. If the server cannot determine the state of the token without more information, it SHOULD return a response saying the token is not active.

To prevent token scanning attacks, the endpoint MUST also require some form of authorization to access it, such as client authentication or a separate OAuth 2.0 access token such as a bearer token.
sections.plainLanguage: The call is a form POST that carries the token and, optionally, a hint about what kind of token it is. The server must be authorized for the call, or someone could use it to guess valid tokens one after another.

sections.title: The Introspection Response
sections.content:
The server answers with a JSON object in application/json format. The active member is required and is a boolean saying whether the presented token is currently active. The specifics depend on what the server keeps about its tokens, but a true value generally means the token was issued by this server, has not been revoked by the resource owner, and is within its window of validity.

The rest of the members are optional. scope is a space-separated list of the scopes associated with the token. client_id identifies the client that requested the token. username is a human-readable identifier for the resource owner who authorized it. token_type is the type of the token. exp is the timestamp, in seconds since January 1 1970 UTC, when the token expires. iat is the timestamp when it was originally issued. nbf is the timestamp before which it is not to be used. sub is the subject, usually a machine-readable identifier of the resource owner. aud is a string or list of strings naming the intended audience. iss names the issuer. jti is a string identifier for the token. These time and claim names are the ones defined for a JSON Web Token.

Implementations MAY add their own service-specific members at the top level, but names meant to be used across domains MUST be registered in the OAuth Token Introspection Response registry. The server MAY answer differently to different protected resources asking the same question, for example by limiting which scopes a given resource is told about, so that it does not learn more about the wider network than it needs to run.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is one JSON object. One field says whether the token is live; the rest are optional details such as the user, the client, the permissions and the expiry time.

sections.title: Errors and the Inactive Token
sections.content:
If the protected resource authenticates with OAuth 2.0 client credentials and those credentials are invalid, the authorization server answers with HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) as described in OAuth 2.0. If the protected resource authorizes its call with an OAuth 2.0 bearer token and that token does not carry sufficient privileges or is otherwise invalid for the request, the server answers with HTTP 401 as described in OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token Usage.

A properly formed and authorized query about a token that is inactive, that does not exist on the server, or that the protected resource is not allowed to introspect is not an error. In those cases the server MUST return an introspection response with the active field set to false. To avoid disclosing too much about the server's state to a third party, the response SHOULD NOT carry any further information about an inactive token, including the reason it is inactive.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad call gets an error. A good call about a token that is not valid is not an error: the answer simply says the token is inactive, with no explanation, so that the server does not leak what it knows.

sections.title: Who May Ask and What the Server Must Check
sections.content:
There are many valid ways to implement an OAuth 2.0 system, and therefore many ways for an authorization server to decide whether a token is active. Since resource servers using introspection rely on the server to determine the state of a token, the authorization server MUST perform all the checks that apply to the token. These include whether the token has expired, if it can expire; whether its valid period has started, if it can be issued before it is usable; whether it has been revoked, if it can be revoked after issue; whether the signature is valid, if the token has been signed; and whether it can be used at the particular resource server making the call, if it is restricted to certain resource servers. Not every check applies to every deployment, and it is up to the server to decide which apply.

If the server skips a check that applies, the resource server could make a wrong security decision based on the response. If the endpoint were left unprotected and unthrottled, it would let an attacker poll possible token values and fish for a valid one. The server MUST therefore require authentication of protected resources that need to reach the endpoint, and SHOULD require protected resources to be specifically authorized to call it. The credentials could be any client authentication mechanism used with the token endpoint, an OAuth 2.0 access token, or another HTTP authorization mechanism. Software that acts as both a client and a protected resource may reuse the same credentials for the token endpoint and the introspection endpoint, though that conflates the two roles and the server may require separate credentials.

Because the endpoint takes tokens as parameters and returns information used for authorization decisions, the server MUST support TLS 1.2 and MAY support other transport-layer mechanisms that meet its requirements. When using TLS, the client or protected resource MUST check the server certificate. To keep token values out of server-side logs, a server offering introspection MAY disallow HTTP GET on the endpoint and require POST instead.

A protected resource MAY cache the response, which improves performance and reduces load on the endpoint, at the cost of the freshness of the information used for authorization decisions. A short cache timeout gives fresher information at the cost of more traffic and load; a longer one does the opposite but risks stale information, for example a token that was revoked while the resource relied on the cached answer. That creates a window in which a revoked token could still be used, so the acceptable cache duration has to be chosen with the sensitivity of the resource in mind. Sensitive environments can disable caching entirely. If the response contains the exp parameter, the response MUST NOT be cached beyond that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to do the real checks itself, since the resource server trusts its answer. And the answer can be cached, which saves traffic but means a revoked token may still work for a while.

sections.title: Privacy of the Answer
sections.content:
The introspection response may contain privacy-sensitive information such as user identifiers for resource owners. When it does, measures MUST be taken to prevent that information from reaching unintended parties. One method is to transmit user identifiers as opaque service-specific strings, potentially returning a different identifier to each protected resource.

If the protected resource sends additional information about the client's request to the authorization server, such as the client's IP address, using an extension of this specification, that extension has privacy considerations of its own which it should detail. The nature of such extensions is outside the scope of this specification.

Omitting privacy-sensitive information from an introspection response is the simplest way of minimizing the privacy issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer can name the user, so it can be private information. The simplest protection is not to include it, and another is to give each service its own opaque name for the same person.

sections.title: The Response Name Registry
sections.content:
This specification establishes the OAuth Token Introspection Response registry, where the top-level names of the introspection response are recorded. Names are registered after a two-week review period on the OAuth extensions review mailing list, on the advice of one or more Designated Experts, and the Designated Experts may approve a registration once they are satisfied that the specification will be published, which allows names to be allocated before publication.

Each registration has a name, which is case sensitive and should not match an existing name in a case-insensitive way, a description of the metadata value, a change controller, which is the IETF for Standards Track documents, and a reference to the document or documents that specify the token endpoint authorization method. Names that match claims in the JSON Web Token Claims registry should have comparable definitions and semantics.

The initial contents of the registry are active, username, client_id, scope, token_type, exp, iat, nbf, sub, aud, iss and jti, each with a one-line description and a pointer to Section 2.2 of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Any new field that should work across different services has to be registered, so that everyone means the same thing by the same name.

messages.label: POST /introspect
messages.note: Form-encoded body with the token, and optional token_type_hint. The call must be authorized.

messages.label: 200 OK, application/json
messages.note: The active field, plus optional scope, client_id, username and timestamps.

messages.label: 401 Unauthorized
messages.note: When the call itself is not properly authorized.
